topic: Course Overview, What is Calculus & Functions
core_points: Calculus comes from the Latin word for 'pebble' (ancient counting tool).
Calculus deals with dynamic change and motion, contrasting static algebra.
Real number line: continuous points from -∞ to +∞.
Functions: y = f(x) where x is input and y is output.

pillars.name: Differential Calculus
pillars.desc: Splitting quantities into infinitesimally small pieces to compute rates of change.

pillars.name: Integral Calculus
pillars.desc: Accumulating and summing small pieces to evaluate total areas and volumes.

practice_problems: Review real line intervals, domain, and range.

deep_dive.content: Elementary algebra and geometry solve problems involving constant rates and static configurations (such as constant velocity d = vt or the area of flat polygons). Calculus introduces the mathematics of change by approximating non-linear, dynamic processes with linear tangents through limit processes.

A function f from a domain set D to a target set Y is a rule that assigns exactly one output f(x) to each input x. Graphically, this uniqueness condition is verified by the Vertical Line Test: no vertical line x = a may intersect the curve at more than one point.

topic: Real Numbers, Intervals, Absolute Value & Inequalities
core_points: The Real Number System: Natural numbers, Integers, Rationals, and the continuous real line (-∞ to +∞)
Three Core Properties of R: Algebraic properties, Order properties, and the Completeness property
Intervals (Finite vs. Infinite): Open, closed, and half-open subsets across set notation, interval notation, and graphical representation
Absolute Value (|x|): Geometric interpretation as distance from the origin and piecewise algebraic definition
Inequality Rules: Preserving direction under addition/subtraction, reversing direction when multiplying/dividing by negatives, and solving linear inequalities

deep_dive.section: 1. Number System Hierarchy & The Axiom of Completeness
deep_dive.content: Numbers progress through nested subsets: Natural (N) ⊂ Integers (Z) ⊂ Rationals (Q) ⊂ Reals (R). While rational numbers are dense on the line (infinitely many fractions lie between any two numbers), Q contains infinitely many gaps (e.g., √2, e, π). The Completeness Axiom guarantees that the real line has zero missing points: every non-empty subset of R bounded above has a least upper bound (supremum) in R. Calculus limits depend directly on this unbroken continuum.

Algebraically, |x| is defined piecewise as x if x ≥ 0, and -x if x < 0. Geometrically, |a - b| measures the Euclidean 1D distance between points a and b on the real coordinate axis. An inequality like |x - c| < δ defines an open symmetric neighborhood (c - δ, c + δ) centered at c with radius δ—the exact structural formulation used in the formal (ε, δ) definition of limits.

Inequalities preserve their direction under addition and subtraction (a < b implies a + c < b + c). However, multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative scalar (c < 0) reverses the relation: a < b becomes ac > bc. Geometrically, multiplying by a negative number reflects points across the origin (0), which swaps their relative order on the axis.
